The Work, Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Avraham Zacut: Between Spiritual Leadership and a Scientific and Historiographical Revolution
His Life and the Historical Background: From the Golden Age to the Close of the Decrees of Expulsion
Rabbi Avraham ben Shmuel Zacut (c. 1452–1515) was active in one of the most turbulent and critical periods in the history of the people of Israel and of the Western world, in which the tidings of the scientific Renaissance met the tragic decline of Spanish Jewry [cite: 1, 2]. He was born in the city of Salamanca in the kingdom of Castile (present-day Spain) to a distinguished rabbinic family with deep roots in the Iberian Peninsula, which had moved to Spain following the expulsion of the Jews from France in 1306 [cite: 1, 2]. The forefathers of the family were among the Torah leaders of their generation, and one of his ancestors composed the "Sefer HaMishpatim" as early as 1311 [cite: 2]. Zacut's brother-in-law was the Kabbalist Rabbi Avraham ben Eliezer HaLevi, a fact that points to the rich spiritual and Kabbalistic environment in which he grew up [cite: 2].
Zacut grew up in Salamanca, which was at that time one of the leading academic and Torah centres in Europe [cite: 1, 3]. Alongside his deep Torah studies, he advanced his studies and even taught astronomy and mathematics at the University of Salamanca, and afterwards also taught at the universities and scientific centres in Saragossa and Cartagena [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Alongside his scientific activity he served as rabbi of the community and as a recognized halakhic authority [cite: 2].
The dramatic turning point in his life occurred in 1492, with the publication of the Alhambra Decree by the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, who ordered the expulsion of all the Jews from the territories of Spain [cite: 1, 2]. Like many of his brethren, Rabbi Avraham Zacut turned to neighbouring Portugal [cite: 1, 2]. Thanks to his vast scientific output and the reputation he had acquired as a first-rate astronomer, King João II received him at his court and appointed him royal astronomer and historiographer [cite: 1, 2]. In this role he served as a senior adviser in planning the kingdom's maritime voyages of discovery, and in particular in examining the feasibility of finding a sea route to India [cite: 1].
The period of grace in Portugal was short. With the accession of King Manuel I and his demand to marry the daughter of the monarchs of Spain, decrees of conversion and expulsion were imposed on the Jews of Portugal at the end of 1496 [cite: 1, 4]. Rabbi Avraham Zacut refused to convert, and managed to escape with his life and flee to Tunis in North Africa [cite: 1, 5]. During his stay in Tunis he composed his monumental historical work, "Sefer Yuchasin" [cite: 2, 5]. In his final years he moved to the territories of the Ottoman Empire and went up to Eretz Israel, and according to various sources he died in Jerusalem or in Damascus around the year 1515, remaining faithful to his faith and his heritage [cite: 1, 2, 4].
The central stations in the life of Rabbi Avraham Zacut reflect the upheaval that passed over Spanish Jewry in the transition from a cultural centre to the close of the exile: Salamanca until 1492, where his central scientific works were written [cite: 1, 2] -> Lisbon between 1492 and 1497, where he served as royal seer and guide of the Portuguese fleet [cite: 1, 2] -> Tunis from 1497, where "Sefer Yuchasin" was written [cite: 2, 5] -> and finally Jerusalem and Damascus, where he closed the book of his spiritual life [cite: 1, 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers, His Torah Nourishment and the Integration of Torah and Science
The teaching of Rabbi Avraham Zacut was founded on a conception that sees science as a complementary link in the understanding of the Torah and halakha. His distinguished teacher in Torah was Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab ("the last Gaon of Castile"), one of the greatest sages of Spain in the generation of the Expulsion and one of the heads of the yeshivot in Toledo [cite: 3, 6, 7]. Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab was a disciple of Rabbi Yitzchak Canpanton, the revered spiritual leader of Spanish Jewry in the fifteenth century [cite: 3, 8]. In "Sefer Yuchasin" Zacut attests with reverence that he merited to see Rabbi Yitzchak Canpanton when he was about six or seven years old, an experience that left a vast impression on him for all his life [cite: 3, 8].
Zacut departed from the conception that saw the study of the sciences as a separate link from the study of the sacred. In the introduction to his works he emphasized that all of his astronomical work and the complex mathematical calculations he performed were intended only to serve a Torah purpose: "to understand the words of the Sages and the halakhot they wrote on this" [cite: 3]. His intention was to delve into difficult issues of fixing the Hebrew calendar, the intercalation of the year, the calculation of the molad of the moon, the laws of the sanctification of the month and the times of the day in halakha [cite: 3]. Before he set about composing his central astronomical work at the age of 21, he took care to ascertain that there was no halakhic prohibition whatsoever in analysing the orbits of the sun and the moon [cite: 9].
This conception reflects the foundations of the thought of the sages of Spain, who saw the external sciences as an auxiliary tool for understanding the wisdom of the Torah. Zacut's brilliant scientific engagement did not come at the expense of his halakhic commitment; he served as rabbi of the community and as a recognized halakhic authority, and his Torah knowledge was renowned among the sages of his generation [cite: 1, 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Astronomical Work and the Technological-Maritime Innovation
The scientific works of Rabbi Avraham Zacut changed the face of seafaring and world trade at the end of the fifteenth century and constituted a scientific foundation for the Age of Discovery [cite: 1, 2, 4].
"HaChibbur HaGadol" and the Perpetual Star Tables
At only 25 years of age (in 1478) Zacut completed in Salamanca his important astronomical work in the Hebrew language: "HaChibbur HaGadol" (The Great Composition) [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The work comprised 19 chapters and 65 detailed astronomical tables (ephemerides) based on a base year (the meridian) of Salamanca from 1473 [cite: 1, 2, 9, 10]. These calculations were based on a combination and improvement of the "Alfonsine Tables" (from the school of King Alfonso X) and astronomical works from the Majorcan school of the 14th century [cite: 1, 2, 10].
Zacut calculated with unprecedented accuracy the positions of the sun, the moon and five planets [cite: 1, 2, 10]. The uniqueness of the work lay in the structure of the "perpetual almanac" that he developed, which allowed sailors and astronomers to calculate easily and quickly the position of the heavenly bodies by means of simple interpolation, without the need for complex mathematical calculations in real time [cite: 1, 2].
The book was translated into Castilian in 1481 by Juan de Salaya [cite: 1, 2]. Later, Zacut's disciple, the physician and astronomer Joseph Vizinho (Mestre José Vizinho), translated the work into Latin and Portuguese under the name Tabulae tabularum Celestium motuum sive Almanach perpetuum ("Tables of the Heavenly Motions, or the Perpetual Almanac," also known as "Biur Luchot") [cite: 1, 2]. The tables were brought to print in the city of Leiria in Portugal in 1496, by a Hebrew printing house with movable type – and were among the first books printed in that country [cite: 1, 2, 4].
The chain of translation of "HaChibbur HaGadol" constitutes a clear example of the transmission of scientific knowledge from the Hebrew world of codification to Western culture: the original, written in Hebrew in Salamanca in 1478, was first translated into Castilian (1481), and afterwards translated into Latin and Portuguese by Joseph Vizinho and printed in Leiria (1496), where it became a foundational book for the sailors of Europe [cite: 1, 2, 4].
The Maritime Metal Astrolabe and the Tables of the Sun's Declination
Until Zacut's time, navigators sailed on the open sea mainly by measuring the angle of the North Star above the horizon with the aid of a quadrant [cite: 2]. However, as they sailed south and approached the equator, the North Star disappeared below the horizon, and the navigators were left unable to determine the geographic latitude of their ship [cite: 2, 4].
Rabbi Avraham Zacut solved this problem through two complementary innovations:
1.  Tables of the sun's declination (Solar Declination): Zacut provided accurate tables that made it possible to determine latitude during daylight hours according to the angle of the sun at noon, independently of the North Star [cite: 2, 11].
2.  The maritime metal astrolabe: the traditional astrolabe was a delicate copper or wooden instrument intended for use on land [cite: 1, 2, 9]. Zacut refined the device for maritime use: he replaced the light wooden or wood-and-metal plates with a heavy metal disc (brass/copper) with holes, allowing the wind to pass through it and minimizing the instrument's oscillations on the deck of a tossing ship [cite: 1, 2, 9]. The combination of the maritime astrolabe with Zacut's declination tables made it possible to read the angle of the sun with high accuracy in mid-ocean [cite: 2, 9].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Encounter with the Explorers and the Influence on the Age of Discovery
The discoveries and calculations of Rabbi Avraham Zacut were a key component in the success of the voyages of the greatest explorers.
Vasco da Gama and the Way to India
In 1496, ahead of Vasco da Gama's departure on the historic voyage to discover the sea route to India, King Manuel I summoned Rabbi Avraham Zacut to brief the admiral and his crew [cite: 1, 2, 11]. Zacut provided the expedition with his navigation tables, trained the sailors in the use of the new maritime metal astrolabe, and gave Vasco da Gama maps and astronomical instruments [cite: 2, 4, 11]. Thanks to these tools da Gama succeeded in navigating safely in the South Atlantic Ocean and the Indian Ocean, and in completing the voyage that changed the map of world trade [cite: 2, 11].
Christopher Columbus and the Solar Eclipse Incident
Christopher Columbus held a copy of Zacut's "Perpetual Almanac" and used it continuously on his voyages to America [cite: 1, 2, 9]. Columbus's journals attest to the decisive usefulness of the tables in calculating his position in the ocean [cite: 9].
A famous incident that occurred in 1504 on the island of Jamaica illustrates the accuracy of Zacut's tables [cite: 2, 3]. Columbus and his crew fell into severe food shortage and a bloody conflict with the local natives, who refused to supply them with provisions [cite: 2, 3]. Columbus consulted Zacut's astronomical tables and saw that a lunar (or solar) eclipse was expected to occur that night [cite: 2, 3]. He threatened the native leaders that if they did not supply food, he would extinguish the light of the moon [cite: 2, 3]. When the eclipse began precisely at the calculated hour, the natives were seized with fear, complied with all of Columbus's demands and saved his crew from the disgrace of starvation [cite: 2, 3].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"Sefer Yuchasin" and the Historiographical Methodology
Alongside his scientific work, Rabbi Avraham Zacut is regarded as one of the pioneers of Jewish historiography in the early modern period. His great historical work, "Sefer Yuchasin," was written during his stay in Tunis after the Expulsion, and was first printed in Constantinople in the year 5326 (1566) by Shmuel Shulam [cite: 12, 13, 14].
The Structure of the Work
The book is intended to recount the chain of the reception and transmission of the Torah from Moses our teacher, through the period of the Judges, the Kings, the Men of the Great Assembly, the Tannaim, the Amoraim, the Savoraim, the Geonim and the Rishonim, up to the generation of the author [cite: 13, 14].
The work is divided into six main treatises [cite: 13]:
1.  First treatise: the history of the Tannaim, the order of their generations, their disputes and the chain of transmission of the Mishnah [cite: 13].
2.  Second treatise: the order of the Amoraim in Babylonia and Eretz Israel and the dates of the closing of the Talmud [cite: 13].
3.  Third treatise: the period of the Savoraim and the Geonim until the days of the Rif and the Rambam [cite: 13].
4.  Fourth treatise: the chain of the rabbis of France, Ashkenaz, Spain and Provence (the period of the Rishonim) [cite: 13].
5.  Fifth treatise: documentation of the horrors and decrees that befell the people of Israel, and in particular the events of the expulsion from Spain and Portugal [cite: 13].
6.  Sixth treatise: a chronological survey of the history of the nations of the world, the kings of the nations and the development of the sciences [cite: 13].
The Historiographical Method and Source Criticism
Zacut employed an advanced historical methodology, combining fidelity to the Torah tradition with established critical and chronological tools of analysis:
* Cross-referencing primary sources: Zacut relied on ancient texts such as the "Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon," "Seder Olam Rabbah and Zuta," and the "Sefer HaKabbalah" of the Ravad [cite: 13]. He compared versions and synchronized Hebrew dates with general chronologies.
* Preserving rare sources and hidden manuscripts: Zacut incorporated into his book fragments from rare manuscripts that were in his possession and were lost over the years. Particularly famous is the testimony of Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre concerning the sources of the Zohar, which has survived solely thanks to its citation in the first edition of "Sefer Yuchasin" [cite: 12].
* A comprehensive historical conception: Zacut did not isolate Jewish history from general history, but examined the development of the Jewish communities against the background of the political and cultural processes in Europe and the Middle East [cite: 13].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Disciples, His Influence and His Legacy for the Generations
His Disciples and Direct Influence
The most prominent of Zacut's disciples in the scientific field was Joseph Vizinho (José Vizinho), an astronomer, physician and courtier in the kingdom of Portugal [cite: 2, 11]. Vizinho continued the path of his teacher, translated his tables and was a member of the "Junta" (the royal scientific committee) that approved the Portuguese voyages of discovery [cite: 2, 11]. Another important disciple in the Torah world who was influenced by the tradition of study of his study hall (through Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab) was Rabbi Yaakov Berab, the reviver of semikhah in Safed [cite: 7, 15].
The Historical Paradox and the Irony of the Age of Discovery
The life story of Rabbi Avraham Zacut contains a piercing historical paradox. The Iberian powers – Spain and Portugal – profited to an unprecedented degree from Zacut's scientific developments, which opened to them the gates of the oceans and turned them into rich world empires [cite: 2, 4]. Nevertheless, those same kingdoms expelled, persecuted and forced to convert the brethren of the man who gave them the maritime road map [cite: 1, 2, 4]. As the matter has been phrased in historical research: "They kept the map, but expelled the mapmaker" [cite: 4].
Modern Commemoration
The legacy of Rabbi Avraham Zacut as a philosopher, astronomer and historian has received wide international recognition, which also includes modern astronomical awareness:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary and Conclusions
The work and teaching of Rabbi Avraham Zacut represent a peak of Judeo-Spanish culture at the end of the Middle Ages. His figure embodies a unique synthesis between deep Torah devotion and groundbreaking scientific excellence.
As an astronomer, Zacut brought about a revolution in maritime navigation. The development of the maritime metal astrolabe and his tables of the sun's declination (the "Perpetual Almanac") were the technological engine behind the voyages of Vasco da Gama and Christopher Columbus, and made him one of the fathers of the Age of Geographic Discovery [cite: 1, 2, 4, 9, 11].
As a historian, he gave the Jewish people, in the hour of its destruction and dispersion, "Sefer Yuchasin" – a comprehensive historiographical work that ensured the continuity of national memory and preserved the chain of transmission of the Oral Torah amid the storm of the Expulsion and exile [cite: 4, 13, 14].
Rabbi Avraham Zacut remains an exemplary figure of a universal sage, who even in a time of harsh decrees and persecutions did not abandon his faith, and left an indelible mark both on the Jewish bookshelf and on the map of world science and civilization [cite: 2, 4].
